hints: Think about what the word power tells you in everyday life - a more powerful motor does the same job faster, so what two quantities must be compared?
walkthrough:
**What Power Really Means**
Power is all about how quickly energy is moved from one place to another. Doing a lot of work is one thing, but doing it quickly needs more power. So you compare the work done $W$ with the time $t$ taken to do it.

**Exact Definition**
In symbols this is $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ In words: power is work done per unit time, which is the same as rate of energy transfer. The SI unit is the watt, $\text{W}$, where $1\text{ W} = 1\text{ J s}^{-1}$.
Final answer: Power is the work done per unit time, or the rate of transfer of energy.

hints: Start from your definition linking $P$, $W$ and $t$, and think how $W$ is related to the force and the displacement along the force, and how $x$ and $t$ are related for steady motion.
Write $W$ in terms of $F$ and $x$, substitute into $P = W/t$, then simplify the $x/t$ part using constant velocity.
walkthrough:
**Write Down The Two Starting Ideas**
Work done by a force along its direction is force times displacement: $$W = Fx$$ Your definition of power is: $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ Put them together by replacing $W$: $$P = \frac{Fx}{t}$$

**Spot The Velocity**
The object moves with constant velocity $v$ in the direction of $F$, so displacement per unit time is the velocity: $$v = \frac{x}{t}$$ Therefore $$P = F \times \frac{x}{t} = Fv$$ That is the power transferred by the force.
Final answer: $W = Fx$ and $P = W/t$ so $P = Fx/t = Fv$ since $v = x/t$.

hints: The block slides at constant velocity with no friction, so the pull up the slope must exactly balance something pulling down the slope - think which part of the weight acts down the slope.
Resolve the 430 N weight parallel to the 11 degree slope using sine of the angle, then equate that to the tension.
walkthrough:
**Why Tension Equals Part Of The Weight**
Constant velocity means zero resultant force. With no resistive forces, the only force down the slope is the component of weight down the slope. So tension up the slope must balance it exactly.

**Resolve The Weight**
Weight acts vertically down. Its component parallel to a slope at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal is $W \sin\theta$. Here: $$T = W \sin 11^{\circ} = 430 \times \sin 11^{\circ}$$ $$T \approx 430 \times 0.191 = 82\text{ N}$$ to 2 s.f.

hints: You now know the useful power and the force doing the useful work along the motion - recall the link from part (a) that connects power, force and speed and think which value to rearrange for.
walkthrough:
**Use Power To Get Speed**
The useful power pushing the block is $P = Tv$, where $T$ acts in the direction of motion. You know $P = 56\text{ W}$ and $T \approx 82\text{ N}$ from (b)(i). Rearrange before putting numbers in: $$v = \frac{P}{T}$$

**Calculate**
$$v = \frac{56}{82} \approx 0.68\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This is slow and steady, as expected for a small power lifting a heavy weight.

hints: Think about what kinetic energy depends on, and what is special about the way this block moves up the slope.
walkthrough:
**Where Does The Work Go?**
The motor does work on the block. In general that work could increase kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, increase gravitational potential energy $mgh$, and do work against friction. Here friction is zero.

**Constant Speed Means No Extra Kinetic Energy**
Because $v$ stays the same, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ stays the same. So all the useful work goes into gravitational potential energy only. That is why rate of gain of potential energy equals the 56 W useful power.
Final answer: The speed (velocity) is constant so there is no change in kinetic energy of the block.

hints: Efficiency tells you the useful 56 W is only 80% of what goes in - think whether the input power must be larger or smaller than 56 W and how to find it.
Once you have the input power, link the given 1.2 kJ input energy to time using power as energy per unit time, remembering to convert kJ to J.
walkthrough:
**Find The Input Power**
Efficiency is useful output divided by total input: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}$$ So the input must be bigger than the output: $$P_{in} = \frac{P_{out}}{0.80} = \frac{56}{0.80} = 70\text{ W}$$

**Convert Energy To Time**
Power is also energy per unit time, $P = E/t$. The input energy is $1.2\text{ kJ} = 1200\text{ J}$. Rearrange: $$t = \frac{E_{in}}{P_{in}} = \frac{1200}{70} \approx 17\text{ s}$$
Final answer: Input power $= 56/0.80 = 70\text{ W}$, time $= 1200/70 = 17\text{ s}$.
